overview: NameProtect is a render-only module whose entire implementation is a static enabled flag. The real behavior lives in the client's custom TTF font renderer: TTFFontRenderer.drawString replaces every occurrence of the player's own name in any string it renders with 'Rise User' while the flag is set, which covers nametags, chat lines and HUD text that route through the renderer. The module sends no packets and rewrites no incoming packets; the server already knows the name because it authored the messages. The C17 chip is the identity-carrying payload family the module is often grouped with, but the module never touches it.

sections.p: The module body is a boolean: onEnable sets the public static enabled flag, onDisable clears it, and nothing else exists. Rise's font pipeline reads the flag directly: TTFFontRenderer.drawString checks NameProtect.enabled at three call sites and substitutes the player name before the glyph pass. The sibling Streamer module follows the same pattern with a player list, replacing each listed name with 'Player'. The module is registered in ProtectedLaunch's module array like every other Rise module.

The substitution is a regex replace: text.replaceAll(mc.thePlayer.getName(), "Rise User"). Because the name is treated as a regular expression pattern, a player name containing metacharacters such as a dot or a dollar sign makes the pattern malformed and the render call throws PatternSyntaxException, breaking the draw path for that frame; the module is only safe for plain alphanumeric names. The replacement applies anywhere the name appears in rendered strings, so nametags, the chat feed and scoreboard-style HUD lines all show the alias.

Nothing leaves the client and no inbound packet is modified: the S02 chat messages, S0C spawns and S3F team updates that carry the name pass through untouched, and the server-side identity, used by staff commands, chat formatting and scoreboards, is unaffected. The hiding is purely a local display transformation, which is why every server-side check below is an honest gap.

files.label: NameProtect.java
files.explanation: The module file: the static enabled flag with its enable and disable lifecycle and nothing else. The absence of handlers is the finding; the module is a state switch for the font renderer.

files.label: TTFFontRenderer.java (name substitution)
files.explanation: The consumer: drawString's NameProtect.enabled gates at lines 160, 226 and 356, with the replaceAll substitution to 'Rise User' and the sibling Streamer block that replaces listed names with 'Player'. It is the render pipeline where the alias is applied, which is the entire mechanism of the module.

countering.label: chat Text (outgoing content scoring)
countering.explanation: NCP's chat Text check scores outgoing C01 content: per-word notLetter ratios, squared before weighting, and the letter-count ratio against the 0.5 optimum feed frequency windows that drive textVL toward the captcha chain. NameProtect rewrites only the rendered form of incoming S02 text, so the check never sees the substitution and the outgoing stream is byte-identical. The entry is an honest gap that documents where name handling does and does not live.

countering.label: chat Captcha (exact-match gate)
countering.explanation: Captcha is an exact-match gate on the outgoing answer message when a captcha challenge is armed. The display-only alias has no influence on the wire message, so the gate behaves exactly as if the module were off. The name-hiding feature can neither help nor hurt captcha completion, which is the honest statement for this entry.

countering.label: ChatUtility (formatter, not a check)
countering.explanation: ChatUtility is the only chat-related file Arc v2 contributes to the S02 corpus, and it is not a check: it centers chat lines by padding with spaces around a fixed CENTER_PX 154 pixel width. There is no Arc v2 consumer of the name surface at all, so the module has no Arc-side exposure beyond this resolving rel, which is the honest gap statement.

countering.label: PacketConverter8 (C17 protocol conversion)
countering.explanation: Hawk's only C17-corpus file is the protocol converter: PacketConverter8 translates custom-payload packets between 1.7 and 1.8 layouts, channel remapping and byte payload repacking, with no content or identity validation. Hawk ships no chat-content or name check anywhere in the corpus, so the module is invisible to Hawk by construction; this entry documents the closest Hawk file and why it does not apply.
